about: The published decryptors Lazarus knows about, kept by hand and checked against each publisher's own page and the No More Ransom project (nomoreransom.org). An entry ships only when its source could be verified; the day it was last checked is in the entry. Lazarus does not download decryptors — the owner fetches the tool from the publisher, and Lazarus runs it on copies.

entries.conditions: Works only when the files were locked with an offline key — a shared key this tool already holds. Files locked with an online key, made for one victim alone, cannot be opened by this tool or honestly by anyone. For older STOP/Djvu (before August 2019), a matched pair of one locked file and its exact original can sometimes help. STOP/Djvu has used hundreds of extensions over the years; the ones listed here are the common signs, not the whole list.
entries.credit: Published free of charge by Emsisoft. The publisher provides the tool as-is, without warranty, and offers support only to customers of a paid Emsisoft product (the publisher's terms).

entries.conditions: Covers GandCrab versions 1, 4, and 5 up to 5.2. The tool needs at least one of the ransom notes the malware left — the note carries part of what it needs to work out the key — so do not let a cleanup tool delete the notes first. It also needs an internet connection while it runs.
entries.credit: Published free of charge by Bitdefender, working with Europol, the Romanian Police, and DIICOT; also listed by the No More Ransom project.
entries.publisher: Bitdefender, with Europol, the Romanian Police, and DIICOT

entries.conditions: Built from the keys the Avaddon group itself released when it shut down in June 2021, so it covers the victims those keys belong to. Avaddon gives each victim's files an extension that can differ from one victim to the next; .avdn is the common one. The tool can take up to a minute on the first file while it finds the right key.
entries.credit: Published free of charge by Emsisoft. The publisher provides the tool as-is, without warranty (the publisher's terms).

entries.conditions: Only for files locked before 13 July 2021: the keys Bitdefender holds cover attacks up to that date, not after it. REvil gives each victim's files a different random extension, so extensions cannot identify it — the *-readme.txt ransom note is the only outward sign, and that pattern alone is weak evidence.
entries.credit: Published free of charge by Bitdefender, built with a law-enforcement partner; also listed by the No More Ransom project.

entries.conditions: Built from Babuk's own source code, which leaked in September 2021 together with some of its keys, and updated with keys recovered since — including the Tortilla variant's. It covers the keys Avast holds; a victim whose key is not among them cannot be helped by it.
entries.credit: Published free of charge by Avast, on a page that lists the signs of each family it covers; the Babuk tool was updated with keys recovered by Cisco Talos and the Dutch police. Also listed by the No More Ransom project.

entries.conditions: One tool covers all three families, made possible when their keys were released publicly in February 2022. These families give each victim's files a random extension, so Lazarus identifies them by the ransom note, DECRYPT-FILES.txt. The decryptor needs a ransom note to rebuild the key before it can start.
entries.credit: Published free of charge by Emsisoft; the source above is the publisher's own step-by-step guide for the tool. The publisher provides the tool as-is, without warranty (the publisher's terms).
